explanations.explanation: Simon Peter says it plain: "I am going fishing." (John 21:3) And the others answer, "We will go with you…" and off they go to the boat. I'd love to have friends who say yes like that when I say I'm heading out.

Jerusalem is a good guess, friend, but this scene happens by the Sea of Tiberias (John 21:1). Nobody packs a bag for a long walk here. Peter says, "I am going fishing." and that's the plan (John 21:3).

No mountain in this scene, friend. They're by the Sea of Tiberias (John 21:1), and Peter's plan is right there at the water. He says, "I am going fishing." and the others say, "We will go with you…" (John 21:3)
Nothing. The text says they "…caught nothing that night." (John 21:3) That's a whole night of work with an empty net to show for it. I think that boat had some quiet morning faces on it.
Plenty comes later, friend, but not yet. This part of the story says they "…caught nothing that night." (John 21:3) The big catch is still coming, and it doesn't come from their own night of work.
Dozens is a big number, friend, but that's not how the night went. The text says they "…caught nothing that night." (John 21:3) Not a dozen, not even one. The fish come later in the story.

He calls out, "Children, do you have any fish?" (John 21:5) Simple question, and the answer is a short one: "No." Notice the disciples still don't know who's asking (John 21:4). A stranger on the shore, a question about the catch, and the whole morning is about to change.
That's not what He asks, friend. He calls from the shore, "Children, do you have any fish?" (John 21:5) It's about their night of fishing, and they answer with one word: "No."

explanations.answer: If He can use their boat
explanations.explanation: Fair guess, friend, but that's not what happens here. Jesus is on the shore, and He calls out, "Children, do you have any fish?" (John 21:5) The disciples answer, "No."

True. They tell Him they have no fish, and He says, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some." (John 21:6) Short instruction, big result. I think it's something to see that they do it, since they still don't know who He is (John 21:4).

It's actually true, friend. The disciples answer "No" when He asks about fish, and then He tells them, "Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some." (John 21:5-6) They cast it there, and that's when the net fills up.

explanations.answer: They can't with so many fish
explanations.explanation: That's it. They cast the net where He said, and they "…were unable to haul it in because of the great number of fish." (John 21:6) Empty all night, then too full to lift. That's a whole new problem, and a good one to have.

Empty was the whole night, friend, but that changes here. After they cast on the right side, they "…were unable to haul it in because of the great number of fish." (John 21:6) The net is so full they can't pull it up.

A net that full sounds like it should rip, doesn't it? But that's not what happens here. They're "…unable to haul it in because of the great number of fish." (John 21:6) And later the text points out that the net was not torn (John 21:11).
That's the one, friend. The disciple whom Jesus loved speaks up and tells Peter, "It is the Lord!" (John 21:7) The text doesn't name him here, so I won't either.

Thomas is listed with the group in John 21:2, friend, but that's not the name the text gives for the one who speaks up. It says "…the disciple whom Jesus loved…" tells Peter, "It is the Lord!" (John 21:7) The text doesn't name him here, so I won't either.

Nathanael is listed with the group in John 21:2, friend, so I see why he came to mind. But the text gives a different description for the one who speaks up: "…the disciple whom Jesus loved…" tells Peter, "It is the Lord!" (John 21:7) The text doesn't name him here, so I won't either.

Not quite, friend. Peter does the opposite of staying put. "As soon as Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment (for he had removed it) and jumped into the sea." (John 21:7) The net can wait. He's heading for the shore.

False is right. Peter doesn't stay in the boat. The text says he "…put on his outer garment (for he had removed it) and jumped into the sea." (John 21:7) He hears "It is the Lord!" and moves, no waiting around.

Careful with this one, friend. The text says they were "…not far from land, only about a hundred yards." (John 21:8) That's nowhere near a mile. The others bring in the boat and drag the net full of fish behind them.
False is right. The text says they were "…not far from land, only about a hundred yards." (John 21:8) That's a short trip, not a mile. The others bring the boat in and drag the net of fish ashore.

Close, but Jesus says just the opposite. He tells them, "Bring some of the fish you have just caught." (John 21:10) There's already fish on the fire (John 21:9), and He still asks for theirs. I think that says something nice about how He includes them.

False is right. Even with fish already on the fire (John 21:9), Jesus says, "Bring some of the fish you have just caught." (John 21:10) He doesn't tell them to sit it out. He asks them to bring some of their own catch.
That's the number. The text says the net "…was full of large fish, 153…" (John 21:11) Somebody counted those fish, friend. I get that, because I'd count my cookies too.
120 is a fair guess, friend, but it's not the count here. The net "…was full of large fish, 153…" (John 21:11) That's the number the text gives. And it says they were large fish, too.
That's a nice round number, but the text gets more exact. The net "…was full of large fish, 153…" (John 21:11) Not 200, just 153, and the text says they were large fish too.
Torn is it. The text says, "…even with so many, the net was not torn." (John 21:11) 153 large fish is a lot of weight for one net. The text makes a point of telling us it held.
Tangled sounds like a fair guess with that many fish, but it's not the word here. The text says, "…even with so many, the net was not torn." (John 21:11) The net held up.
Sinking is a fair guess with that load, friend, but it's not the word here. The text says, "…even with so many, the net was not torn." (John 21:11) Torn is the word that fits the blank.

Jesus Himself, friend. The text says, "Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and He did the same with the fish." (John 21:13) He called them to breakfast, and then He's the one who serves them. I think that's a pretty humble way to start a morning.

Peter has plenty to do this morning, like jumping in the sea and dragging the net (John 21:7, 11), but he's not the one serving. The text says, "Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and He did the same with the fish." (John 21:13) That's Jesus Himself handing out the breakfast.

Nathanael is there, listed in John 21:2, but he's not the one handing out breakfast, friend. It's Jesus who "…came and took the bread and gave it to them, and He did the same with the fish." (John 21:13) The One who called them to breakfast is the One who serves it. I'd take a seat at that table fast.

Third, friend. The text says, "This was now the third time that Jesus appeared to the disciples after He was raised from the dead." (John 21:14) So this isn't the first time they've seen Him. The word "now" tells us it's one more appearance added to the ones before.

Second is one short, friend. The text says, "This was now the third time that Jesus appeared to the disciples after He was raised from the dead." (John 21:14) So this breakfast by the sea is number THREE. I spent years in a junk drawer with nothing to do but count dust, and even I can count to three!

Fourth is one too many, friend. The text says, "This was now the third time that Jesus appeared to the disciples after He was raised from the dead." (John 21:14) So this breakfast by the sea is number three.
